Let
LET
verb
From two Old English verbs fallen together: lætan, “to allow,” and lettan, “to hinder, to obstruct” (kin to late). The KJV’s “let” is this second word — to hinder, to restrain — the exact opposite of the modern “let.”

Biblical Definition

Here is a word turned clean about. In modern English to let is to allow; in the Authorized Version to let is to hinder, to restrain, to hold back. The two senses are two different Old English verbs that wore down to the same spelling, and only the older survives in law, where a “let or hindrance” still means an obstruction, and in tennis, where a “let” is a ball hindered by the net. Scripture uses the older sense throughout. Paul tells the Romans he had often purposed to come to them, “but was let hitherto” (Rom 1:13) — hindered, prevented from coming, not permitted. Pharaoh charges Moses and Aaron, “wherefore do ye… let the people from their works?” (Exo 5:4) — why do ye hinder them from their labour? The most weighty use is prophetic: of the mystery of iniquity Paul writes, “only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way” (2Th 2:7) — there is a Restrainer who holds back the man of sin, and lawlessness cannot break loose until that hindering hand is lifted. Set against every human hindrance stands the LORD, whom none can hinder: “I will work, and who shall let it?” (Isa 43:13). There is the comfort. Men are let and hindered at every turn, their best purposes obstructed; but God is never let. His counsel shall stand, His work goes forward, and no power in heaven or earth can restrain the hand that upholds all things.

Webster 1828 Definition

To hinder; to restrain; to obstruct — the reverse of the modern “to allow.”

LET, to hinder; to obstruct; to interpose an impediment; to restrain.

From Old English lettan, “to hinder,” kin to late; distinct from lætan, “to allow.”

It survives in the legal phrase “let or hindrance” and in the game of tennis.

Paul was let — hindered — from coming to Rome (Rom 1:13).

The Restrainer letteth the man of sin until He be taken away (2Th 2:7).

Key Scripture

2Th 2:7 — "For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way."

Rom 1:13 — "Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles."

Isa 43:13 — "Yea, before the day was I am he; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand: I will work, and who shall let it?"

Exo 5:4 — "And the king of Egypt said unto them, Wherefore do ye, Moses and Aaron, let the people from their works? get you unto your burdens."

Modern Corruption

An old word for hindering; it recovers the Restrainer who holds back iniquity, and the LORD whom none can hinder.

expand to see more

The drift here is a true reversal, and it is the most treacherous of the false friends, for the word has come to mean its own opposite. To the modern ear “let” means to permit; in the KJV it means to prevent. A reader who does not know it will take “he who now letteth will let” to mean he who now permits will permit, and lose the whole doctrine of restraint that Paul is teaching. Only the older sense makes sense of the sentence: Someone is hindering the man of sin, and will go on hindering him, until He is taken out of the way. The lawful reader must hold the two lets apart and take the harder, older one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of the Restrainer. The mystery of iniquity is already at work, held in check by a hindering power; when that power withdraws, the lawless one is revealed. Whatever the Restrainer be — the Spirit striving, the preached gospel, lawful magistracy under God — the point stands: evil is not loose in the world to the full of its will, but bridled by a hand it cannot see. And the same hand that lets the wicked cannot itself be let. “I will work, and who shall let it?” No devil hinders God; the God who hinders devils works His whole pleasure unopposed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to hinder, to restrain, to obstruct — not to allow.

expand to see more

Let — Old English lettan, “to hinder,” kin to late.

It is a different verb from lætan, “to allow,” though spelled alike.

The KJV sense is to obstruct or restrain, the reverse of the modern word.

Paul was let — hindered — from coming to Rome (Rom 1:13).

None can let the work of the LORD: “who shall let it?” (Isa 43:13).

Usage

"To let in the KJV is to hinder: Paul “was let hitherto” from coming to Rome."

"He who now letteth will let — the Restrainer hinders iniquity till he be removed."

"“I will work, and who shall let it?” — no power hinders the hand of God."
